provenance.inputs_seen_by_extractor: this evaluation's body text only (no paper, no model output)
provenance.post_check: reviewer-name tokens replaced by [name] after the quote check

issues.text: Missing data handling is improper: studies with non-significant or unreported effects were assigned a fixed SMD of 0.01 with zero imputation variance, which ignores uncertainty, underestimates total variance, over-weights imputed studies, and artificially tightens confidence intervals.
issues.quote: The authors imputed a fixed SMD of 0.01 for such cases.

issues.text: Imputing 0.01 for non-significant studies creates an artificial vertical column of points in the funnel plot, hindering interpretation of the relationship between standard error and effect size.
issues.quote: producing an artificial vertical cluster of points at 0.01 that hinders interpretation of the standard error--effect size relationship

issues.text: Prediction intervals are reported inconsistently across subgroup analyses, which is a missed opportunity given the small mean effect and heterogeneity; their absence hampers judging practical utility of interventions.
issues.quote: Although prediction intervals are mentioned in the main analysis, they are inconsistently reported across subgroup analyses.

issues.text: Confidence intervals are likely to be misread as the full range of plausible effects, which can lead to overconfidence in the precision and direction of results; the evaluator implies prediction intervals would address this.
issues.quote: readers often misinterpret them as indicating the full range of plausible effects, even though true effects may lie well outside that interval

issues.text: Excluding small-sample studies (under 25 per group) is unwarranted; it restricts the range of standard errors, making publication bias harder to detect and correct.
issues.quote: The exclusion of small-sample studies (i.e., \<25 per group) is unwarranted.

issues.text: At least 16 studies were excluded solely for small sample size, based on the evaluator's manual count of the exclusion data.
issues.quote: there were at least 16 studies were excluded solely for having small sample sizes with no other exclusion reasons.

issues.text: Only a single outcome per intervention is extracted, discarding valuable data and reducing statistical power; the hierarchical outcome selection rule introduces selection issues and inconsistent treatment of outcome B across studies.
issues.quote: The authors extract only a single effect per intervention: the outcome with the longest follow-up measuring net MAP or RPM consumption.

issues.text: The outcome selection hierarchy creates a paradox in which an outcome is treated as sufficient evidence in one study but ignored in another when both are available.
issues.quote: This creates a paradox where outcome B is treated as sufficient evidence in one context but ignored in another, even when available.

issues.text: Given the use of multilevel and robust variance methods elsewhere, there is no compelling reason to exclude valid outcome data; all relevant effects should be included with appropriate dependence modelling.
issues.quote: there is no compelling reason to exclude valid outcome data. A more appropriate strategy would be to include all relevant outcomes and effects per study

issues.text: The risk-of-bias assessment is informal and incomplete; it does not use a validated tool such as Cochrane RoB 2 and omits key biases such as selective outcome reporting, attrition, approximated statistics, and lack of blinding.
issues.quote: Instead of using a validated tool such as Cochrane RoB 2.0, the paper restricts itself to meta-regressions based on open data/pre-registration, publication status, and self-report versus objective outcomes.

issues.text: Attrition bias is not addressed in RCTs; included studies rely on complete-case analyses, and the authors should have prioritised intent-to-treat analyses to preserve internal validity.
issues.quote: Many included studies rely on complete-case analyses, ignoring participants who dropped out post-randomization or failed to report outcomes.

issues.text: Effect size coding relies heavily on guesswork and approximation (e.g., approximated SDs, guessed sample sizes, improper conversions, subjective extraction choices), and these uncertainties are not propagated into the analysis, which treats derived estimates as known point values.
issues.quote: As it stands, the meta-analysis appears to treat these derived estimates as fully known point values with sampling error only.

issues.text: Coding notes quoted by the evaluator show that a considerable fraction of the effect size dataset is constructed through improper, approximate, and unsystematic calculations, undermining the validity of the estimates.
issues.quote: These examples suggest that a considerable fraction of the effect size dataset is constructed through improper, approximate, and unsystematic calculations.

issues.text: The literature review is not sufficiently systematic or reproducible: search strategy, inclusion criteria, and screening justifications are not fully documented, Google Scholar precludes reproducible searches, and reliance on prior reviews inherits their unsystematic searches.
issues.quote: The use of Google Scholar precludes reproducible searches.

issues.text: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are referenced inconsistently across the text and code, making it hard to assess whether the evidence base is comprehensive or unbiased.
issues.quote: clearly articulated inclusion and exclusion criteria (which are referenced inconsistently across the text and code)

issues.text: Several key statistical functions are implemented as custom scripts across folders rather than established packages such as metafor, which complicates code tracing and debugging for secondary analysts.
issues.quote: several key statistical functions are implemented as custom scripts across different folders rather than leveraging existing packages (e.g., `metafor`).
